title: A Ton of Gold at the Klondike Mouth
subtitle: The Bonanza strike, the stampede over the passes and the Hän fish camp at Tr'ochëk, Yukon, 1896–1899
intro: In mid-August 1896 a Tagish family party at the mouth of the Klondike River went up a side stream called Rabbit Creek and found gold lying thick in the gravel. The party was Keish (Skookum Jim), his nephew Káa Goox (Dawson Charlie), his sister Shaaw Tláa (Kate Carmack) and her American husband George Carmack. On 17 August the men staked the creek, soon renamed Bonanza, and Carmack's name went on the Discovery claim. Within weeks the miners of Forty Mile and the older creeks had staked everything in reach.

Who found the gold is still disputed, and this chapter treats it as positions with evidence. Carmack later claimed the find. The surveyor William Ogilvie, who interviewed every party, credited Keish with the find on Bonanza and gave the Nova Scotian Robert Henderson, who had sent Carmack into the area but did not want his Tagish companions there, the title of discoverer of the Klondike. Indigenous oral histories credit Shaaw Tláa with the first large nugget. A guidebook of 1897 named only Henderson, and gave a different date.

The camp at the Klondike mouth already belonged to someone. Tr'ochëk was the salmon fishery of the Hän-speaking Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in under Chief Isaac. Their own heritage account says they were forced out within a month of the strike. Over the winter of 1897–98 they moved to Moosehide, three miles downriver, while the town of Dawson spread over the flat beside them. No firsthand account by Chief Isaac from 1896–99 was found. His later words survive as reporters printed them, and his people's memory survives in their own published histories. Both are placed here beside the police reports.

News reached the outside world only in July 1897. The Excelsior docked at San Francisco on 14 July and the Portland at Seattle on 17 July, and the Post-Intelligencer's story of more than a ton of gold set off a stampede in the middle of a depression. Perhaps a hundred thousand people set out and something over thirty thousand passed down the Yukon. They went over the Chilkoot and White Passes, where Superintendent Sam Steele's North-West Mounted Police raised the flag in February 1898 and turned back anyone without a year's food. They built boats at Lakes Lindeman and Bennett and ran the rapids at Miles Canyon. On Palm Sunday, 3 April 1898, avalanches below the Chilkoot summit killed more than sixty people. Ottawa made the Yukon a separate territory on 13 June 1898. Dawson's population peaked that summer (estimates range from under 20,000 to 30,000 or more), and in 1899 the beach gold of Nome began to draw it away.

Most of the record is not diaries. It is a police report, a surveyor's memoir, newspaper extras, a promoter's guidebook, a typed diary kept by one of Jack London's partners, Steele's pocket diary and memoir, and two later memoirs told by a Tagish nephew and a Chicago woman who crossed the pass pregnant. The Tagish and Hän principals left no writing of their own from these years. Their positions come through others, and the chapter says so each time. Read together, the sources show the same claims through each pair of eyes: one creek seen as a family's find, a police registry entry, a promoter's town lots, a newspaper's ton of gold, and a people's lost fishery.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. The find and the staking fall on consecutive days: the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in and Parks Canada give 16 August 1896 for the discovery, and 17 August, the day of staking, is kept in the Yukon as Discovery Day. Joseph Ladue's 1897 guidebook dates the first gold, which it credits to Henderson, to 24 August 1896. Dollar figures are in contemporary US or Canadian dollars at roughly 17 dollars an ounce.

eyes.name: Keish (Skookum Jim Mason)
eyes.role: Tagish man of Tlingit descent, about 41 in 1896; packer on the Chilkoot route, prospector; brother of Kate Carmack
eyes.where: Rabbit (Bonanza) Creek and the fish camp at the Klondike mouth; later Carcross

waypoints.label: Fish camp at the Klondike mouth, July 1896

eyes.vantage_label: the man most historians credit with the find
eyes.authenticity: No diary or letter in his own hand is known. His account of the find survives through William Ogilvie, who interviewed him and Dawson Charlie separately and together (Early Days on the Yukon, 1913), through his nephew Patsy Henderson's later telling, and through Tagish oral history gathered by the Yukon Archives (Skookum Jim oral history project, MSS 254).
eyes.bio: A strong packer on the Chilkoot whose English nickname meant 'strong', Keish went down the Yukon in 1896 partly to look for his sister Shaaw Tláa and her husband. Ogilvie, who knew all the parties, judged him the actual finder on Bonanza and called him truthful. He took a half-interest in the Discovery claim and No. 1 Above, grew rich, and in 1905 put his fortune in trust; after his death in 1916 it supported his family and a trust for Yukon Indigenous people.

sources.title: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Keish (Skookum Jim Mason)
Ogilvie, Early Days on the Yukon (1913), excerpt at Great Unsolved Mysteries in Canadian History

eyes.name: Shaaw Tláa (Kate Carmack)
eyes.role: Tagish woman, mid-thirties in 1896; wife of George Carmack since the late 1880s, mother of their daughter Graphie Grace
eyes.where: The fish camp at the Klondike mouth, then the claims on Bonanza; California; Carcross
eyes.vantage_label: at the fish camp; the disputed co-finder
eyes.authenticity: No surviving firsthand account found. What is known comes from the Dictionary of Canadian Biography (built on Carmack's and Patsy Henderson's accounts and the Yukon Archives oral history material) and from Indigenous oral histories cited by the Canadian Mining Hall of Fame, which inducted her in 2019. Her legal actions against Carmack after 1900 left no recorded words of hers that this chapter could find.
eyes.bio: Shaaw Tláa lost a first husband and infant daughter to influenza before she married George Carmack, and lived with him prospecting and fishing on the Yukon from 1889. Local Indigenous oral histories hold that she found the first large nugget while fetching water; most historians credit her brother. She fed the camp through the first winter, was abandoned by Carmack in California in 1900, returned to Carcross with nothing from the fortune, and died there in the 1920 influenza epidemic.

sources.title: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Shaaw Tláa (Kate Carmack)
Canadian Mining Hall of Fame: Shaaw Tlaa (Kate Carmack), inducted 2019

eyes.name: Koołseen (Patsy Henderson)
eyes.role: Tagish youth, nephew of Keish and Shaaw Tláa, about 17 in 1896
eyes.where: With the search party to the Klondike mouth, summer 1896; later Carcross

waypoints.label: Carcross, departs to find the Carmacks
Carcross, tells the story to visitors for decades

eyes.vantage_label: a boy in the family party
eyes.authenticity: His account, Early Days at Caribou Crossing and the Discovery of Gold on the Klondike, was published in 1950, more than fifty years after the events, from a story he had told many times to tourists at Carcross. It is cited in the Dictionary of Canadian Biography entries on Keish and Shaaw Tláa. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Koołseen travelled down the Yukon with his uncle Keish and Káa Goox in 1896 looking for the Carmacks. He was the youngest of the party and the last survivor of it. His family version names Keish as the finder and keeps alive the Tagish side of a story the newspapers told about Carmack.

sources.title: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Keish (bibliography lists Patsy Henderson's 1950 account)

eyes.name: George Washington Carmack
eyes.role: American prospector and trader, 36 in 1896; married into the Tagish community; credited on paper with the Discovery claim
eyes.where: Fish camp at the Klondike mouth; Bonanza Creek; Forty Mile recording office

waypoints.label: Forty Mile, records the claim 24 September 1896

eyes.vantage_label: the man whose name went on the claim
eyes.authenticity: His own account, My Experiences in the Yukon, was printed privately in 1933, eleven years after his death, by his second wife Marguerite. In it he presents himself as the finder; Ogilvie, who interviewed him and the others, did not accept that. The recording of the claim on 24 September 1896 is documented. Digest only.
eyes.bio: A Californian who came north as a ship's hand and stayed, Carmack lived among the Tagish, married Shaaw Tláa and was mocked by other miners for it. Because the claim was in his name, the outside world called him the discoverer. Within four years the claims had produced close to a million dollars; in 1900 he married a Dawson woman and left Kate in California.

sources.title: Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Keish (on Carmack's recording of the claim)
Parks Canada: Discovery Claim National Historic Site

eyes.name: Robert Henderson
eyes.role: Nova Scotian prospector, 39 in 1896; working Gold Bottom Creek in the Klondike basin since spring 1896
eyes.where: Gold Bottom Creek, a few miles over the divide from Bonanza
eyes.vantage_label: the rival who was not told
eyes.form: petitions and statements recorded by others
eyes.authenticity: No diary. His case survives in the accounts he gave Ogilvie, in lobbying correspondence of 1901–1904 (P. G. Keyes, H. J. Woodside) and in later Historic Sites and Monuments Board files, summarised by Doug Whyte in The Northern Review 19 (1998). He presented himself as the true discoverer; the claim is a position, not a settled fact.
eyes.bio: Henderson had prospected the Indian River country for two years and found paying gold on Gold Bottom. He told Carmack to come and stake, but objected to Carmack's Tagish companions, and they did not send word back when they struck Bonanza. He got only an ordinary claim, sold it to pay medical bills, and spent years petitioning Ottawa, which eventually gave him placer ground and a salaried post in Dawson.

sources.title: Robert Henderson's Search for Recognition (after Whyte, Northern Review 1998)

eyes.name: Chief Isaac
eyes.role: Leader of the Hän-speaking Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in from before the gold rush until his death
eyes.where: Tr'ochëk, the fish camp at the Klondike mouth; then Moosehide, three miles downriver
eyes.vantage_label: the people whose land and fishery it was
eyes.form: reported speech (newspapers) and community heritage accounts
eyes.authenticity: No surviving firsthand account by Chief Isaac from 1896–1899 was found. His later words survive as reporters printed them (Seattle papers 1902; Dawson Daily News, 15 December 1911, printed in dialect), in a missionary's note (Rev. Totty, 1919) and in the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in's own published heritage accounts, which draw on family interviews (his daughter Patricia Lindgren, 1974–75; Percy Henry, 1993). Reporters' renderings may not reflect his own phrasing.
eyes.bio: Isaac was baptised by Bishop Bompas around 1892 and acted as the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in's go-between with miners, police, church and government. Within weeks of the strike his people lost Tr'ochëk to the stampede; by spring 1898 they had moved to Moosehide. His family remembers that he arranged the move to keep his people from the town's bad habits and that he took songs and dances to Alaskan relatives for safekeeping. In later speeches he claimed the land, the game and the gold for his people.

sources.title: Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in: Tr'ochëk
Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in: Chief Isaac (heritage booklet, PDF)
Yukon News: Chief Isaac and the mass media

eyes.name: Charles Constantine
eyes.role: Inspector, North-West Mounted Police, commanding the Yukon detachment at Fort Constantine (Forty Mile), aged 47; acting gold commissioner and dominion agent
eyes.where: Fort Constantine, beside Forty Mile on the Yukon
eyes.vantage_label: the policeman who recorded the claims
eyes.authenticity: His Report on the Yukon Detachment, dated Fort Constantine, 20 November 1896, was printed as Appendix DD of the NWMP annual report for 1896 (Canadian Sessional Papers). Public domain; transcribed by ExploreNorth.
eyes.bio: Constantine had brought twenty police to the Yukon in 1895 to assert Canadian sovereignty over a mining country run by American miners' meetings. He was the officer before whom Carmack recorded the Discovery claim. His November 1896 report is the first official notice of the Klondike: claim counts, values per pan, and an urgent request for a gold commissioner, courts and more men.

sources.title: NWMP Report 1896, Appendix DD (ExploreNorth transcription)
Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Charles Constantine

eyes.name: William Ogilvie
eyes.role: Dominion Land Surveyor, aged 50 in 1896; surveyor of claims and of the Dawson townsite; Commissioner of the Yukon Territory 1898–1901
eyes.where: Forty Mile and the Klondike creeks; Dawson
eyes.vantage_label: the surveyor who judged the dispute
eyes.authenticity: Early Days on the Yukon and the Story of Its Gold Finds (London and Ottawa, 1913, published after his death) draws on his field notes and on interviews with Carmack, Keish, Káa Goox and Henderson. Public domain and quotable. He gives the discovery title to Henderson for the Klondike but credits Keish with the find on Bonanza.
eyes.bio: Ogilvie had surveyed the Yukon and the 141st meridian since 1887 and knew everyone in the country. He resurveyed the overstaked Bonanza claims, set out the Dawson townsite, and later governed the territory. His account of the discovery is the closest thing to a judicial inquiry the episode had, and it is candid about the prejudice against Carmack's Indigenous partners.

sources.title: Early Days on the Yukon (1913), Canadiana scan
Excerpt on the discovery, Great Unsolved Mysteries in Canadian History

eyes.name: Joseph Francis Ladue
eyes.role: American trader and prospector, 41 in 1896; partner of Henderson's grubstake at Ogilvie post; founder of the Dawson townsite
eyes.where: Ogilvie post on the Sixtymile, then the flat at the Klondike mouth
eyes.authenticity: Klondyke Nuggets (New York, 1897) was published under his name as a guide for stampeders and was part promotion; its dating of the first find differs from the others. Public domain (Project Gutenberg 10043) and quotable.
eyes.bio: Ladue had grubstaked Henderson and ran a post up the Sixtymile. When the strike came he staked the flat below the Hän fish camp as a townsite, named it for the geologist George M. Dawson, and sold lots. Back in the United States in 1897 he lent his name to a quickly made guidebook that told readers how to get rich in the Klondike.

sources.title: Klondyke Nuggets (1897), Project Gutenberg 10043

eyes.name: Beriah Brown Jr. (Seattle Post-Intelligencer)
eyes.role: Reporter for the Seattle Post-Intelligencer who met the steamer Portland at sea in a chartered tug
eyes.where: On Puget Sound and at Schwabacher Wharf, Seattle
eyes.vantage_label: the press that made the rush
eyes.authenticity: The Post-Intelligencer's extra of 17 July 1897 is public domain. Its text was reprinted the next day by the Daily Colonist of Victoria (transcribed by ExploreNorth); HistoryLink summarises the reporting and identifies Brown. The famous 'ton of gold' wording comes from the story's text; the main headline cried 'GOLD! GOLD! GOLD! GOLD!'.
eyes.bio: The P-I chartered the tug Sea Lion to reach the Portland before she docked, and Brown came back with the story of sixty-eight miners and a fortune in gold. Telegraphed and reprinted across the continent, it turned a remote Canadian strike into a mass migration in the middle of an economic depression.

sources.title: HistoryLink 687: Portland arrives in Seattle
Daily Colonist, 18 July 1897, reprinting the Post-Intelligencer (ExploreNorth)

eyes.name: Fred Thompson
eyes.role: Member of Jack London's party of stampeders from Oakland and San Francisco, 1897
eyes.where: Dyea, the Chilkoot, Lake Lindeman, down the Yukon to the Stewart River
eyes.authenticity: An 11-page typewritten diary, July–October 1897, survives as a carbon copy with marginal notes by Charmian London in the Jack London Papers at the Huntington Library (JL 1692). The original manuscript was not located. The dates below are those given by the National Park Service's account of London's journey, which follows this diary.
eyes.bio: Thompson travelled with the 21-year-old Jack London, London's brother-in-law James Shepard (who turned back), Merritt Sloper and Jim Goodman. His spare log of landings, portages and boat-building is the dated backbone of London's Klondike year; London himself kept no diary of the outward trip and mined no gold, but the winter at the Stewart gave him his stories.

sources.title: Huntington Library: Thompson diary of Yukon experiences with Jack London (JL 1692)
National Park Service: Gold Rush Writers

eyes.name: Edwin Tappan Adney
eyes.role: American artist and writer, 29, special correspondent for Harper's Weekly
eyes.where: Skagway and the passes, Lake Lindeman, Dawson City 1897–98
eyes.authenticity: His Harper's Weekly dispatches (1897–98) were reworked into The Klondike Stampede (New York, 1900), written from his notes and sketches. Public domain and quotable. Arrival dates follow the Anchorage Daily News review of the reissue.
eyes.bio: Adney was a trained artist and woodsman who later became the great authority on birchbark canoes. He crossed the passes in the autumn rain, built his own boat and reached Dawson as the river froze, then spent a year watching winter mining, food scarcity and the summer boom of 1898. He is the most careful of the stampede's observers.

sources.title: The Klondike Stampede (1900), Internet Archive PDF
Anchorage Daily News on Adney's book (2018)

eyes.name: Samuel Benfield Steele
eyes.role: Superintendent, North-West Mounted Police, aged 49; commanding the posts on the passes and lakes, 1898, then the Yukon force
eyes.where: Skagway, the Chilkoot and White Pass summits, Lake Bennett, Miles Canyon, Dawson
eyes.authenticity: His pocket diary for 1898 is digitised by the University of Alberta's Sir Samuel Steele Collection; it is blank from 20 February to 12 April 1898. His memoir Forty Years in Canada (1915), chapter XV, gives the fuller narrative; it is public domain and quotable but written with hindsight.
eyes.bio: A veteran of the Red River expedition and the North-West, Steele was sent north to hold the border passes for Canada. His men flew the flag at the summits, collected customs and turned back anyone without a year's supplies, then registered and policed the boats on the lakes and the rapids. His diary is terse and administrative; the memoir is proud of the order the police kept.

sources.title: Steele diary 1898 (University of Alberta, Sir Samuel Steele Collection)
Forty Years in Canada (1915), PDF

eyes.name: Martha Louise Munger Purdy Black
eyes.role: Chicago society woman, 32 in 1898, travelling with her brother after her husband abandoned the trip; pregnant on the trail
eyes.where: The Chilkoot Trail and Lake Lindeman, then Dawson City
eyes.authenticity: My Seventy Years (1938, as told to Elizabeth Bailey Price; some sources give 1937) was written forty years after the events and later reissued as My Ninety Years. It is in copyright in many places: digest only. A Yukon Archives scan exists.
eyes.bio: Martha Purdy set out for the Klondike with her husband, who changed his mind in San Francisco; she went on with her brother. She crossed the Chilkoot pregnant, gave birth in a Dawson cabin, stayed, married the lawyer George Black, and in 1935 became the second woman elected to the Canadian House of Commons. Her memoir is the best-known woman's account of the trail.

sources.title: Canadian Encyclopedia: Martha Black
My Seventy Years, Yukon Archives scan (PDF)

entries.place: Fish camp at the mouth of the Klondike (Tr'ochëk)
entries.headline: Three Tagish searchers find the Carmacks fishing for salmon
entries.digest: Having come down the Yukon from the Carcross country, Koołseen, his uncle Keish and Káa Goox found Shaaw Tláa, George Carmack and their three-year-old daughter netting salmon where the Klondike enters the Yukon. The family had been gone for years and the search was partly to bring news of home. The camp they joined sat beside the Hän people's own fishing place.
entries.source_note: Date given as late July 1896 in DCB, Keish and Shaaw Tláa; Patsy Henderson's 1950 account is the family source.

entries.place: Mouth of the Klondike, on a trip for supplies and logs
entries.headline: Henderson tells Carmack where to look, but not his companions
entries.digest: Coming out from Gold Bottom Creek, Henderson met the Carmack party, told them of his prospects over the divide and invited Carmack to stake there. In Ogilvie's account he made it plain that he did not want Carmack's Tagish relatives staking beside him, and later refused to sell Keish tobacco. The party went up Rabbit Creek instead and promised, by Henderson's later telling, to send word if they found anything.
entries.source_note: Ogilvie, Early Days on the Yukon (1913), as excerpted by Great Unsolved Mysteries in Canadian History; Whyte (1998). Day not recorded.

entries.place: Rabbit Creek (renamed Bonanza), a few miles up the Klondike
entries.headline: Waiting by the creek after a moose, Keish sees gold
entries.digest: In the account Ogilvie took down from him, Keish had shot a moose and, while waiting for the others, washed sand in the creek and found gold. Ogilvie judged this the actual discovery on Bonanza. Carmack's later version puts the pan in his own hands. The Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in and Parks Canada give 16 August as the day of the find; the staking followed on 17 August.
entries.source_note: Ogilvie (1913), excerpt at canadianmysteries.ca; Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in Tr'ochëk page (16 Aug); Mining Hall of Fame (17 Aug). The 16/17 split is between find and staking.

entries.place: Rabbit Creek and the fish camp
entries.headline: The family's own memory: a nugget found fetching water
entries.digest: Oral histories told in Yukon Indigenous communities say that Shaaw Tláa found the first large nugget while getting water for tea. Most historians, following Ogilvie, give the find to her brother. No surviving firsthand account by her has been found, so her position survives only through others' tellings.
entries.source_note: Canadian Mining Hall of Fame entry (2019), citing oral histories; DCB, Shaaw Tláa (does not name her as discoverer).

entries.headline: The nephew's version names his uncle
entries.digest: In the story Koołseen told for decades at Carcross and published in 1950, the gold was found by Keish and the men's success depended on Tagish skill at hunting and travel. His telling, like Ogilvie's interviews, makes Carmack the man who put his name on paper rather than the finder.
entries.source_note: Patsy Henderson, Early Days at Caribou Crossing (1950), as cited in DCB, Keish; digest only.

entries.headline: Carmack blazes the Discovery stake in his own name
entries.digest: Carmack insisted on staking the Discovery claim, the double claim the rules allowed the finder, in his own name; Keish took No. 1 Above and Káa Goox No. 2 Below. Ogilvie says Carmack assigned Keish a half-interest in Discovery. Keish stayed behind to guard the stakes while Carmack and Káa Goox set out for Forty Mile to record. No one went back over the hill to tell Henderson.
entries.source_note: Ogilvie (1913) excerpt; canadianmysteries.ca discovery context; DCB, Keish. 17 August is celebrated as Discovery Day.

entries.headline: Keish stays to guard the claims
entries.digest: With the stakes in, Keish remained on the creek to watch over the three claims while his partners went to record them. By Ogilvie's reckoning, the community's prejudice against Carmack's Indigenous partners weighed against Carmack's word, but it also meant that the documents went in a white man's name.
entries.source_note: Ogilvie (1913) excerpt at canadianmysteries.ca.

entries.headline: Within a week the creek is staked and a miners' meeting held
entries.digest: Ogilvie's notes, as he later cited them, record Monahan and Stewart staking on 19 August, Edwards and others on 20 August, and a miners' meeting on the creek on 22 August. Men from Forty Mile and the older creeks abandoned their ground. Many claims were overstaked, which is why his chain and transit were needed that winter.
entries.source_note: Ogilvie, Early Days on the Yukon (1913), dates cited from his notes, via canadianmysteries.ca excerpt.

entries.headline: A guidebook dates the first gold to Henderson
entries.digest: Ladue's Klondyke Nuggets, published the next year, says a man named Henderson found the first gold on 24 August 1896, and does not mention Carmack, Keish or Káa Goox. The book was written for buyers in the United States and sold the country as much as it described it. Its date sits a week after the staking recorded by everyone else.
entries.source_note: Klondyke Nuggets (1897), Project Gutenberg 10043 (statement verified; its accuracy is disputed).

entries.place: The flat at the Klondike mouth, below Tr'ochëk
entries.headline: A townsite staked on the moose pasture
entries.digest: Ladue staked the swampy flat at the mouth of the Klondike as a townsite and named it after the Canadian geologist George M. Dawson. He moved his sawmill there and sold lots. The ground lay beside the Hän fish camp, and the town would grow over it.
entries.source_note: Ladue's role is standard; month approximate. Klondyke Nuggets (1897) and Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in Tr'ochëk page.

entries.date_display: Within a month of the strike, autumn 1896
entries.headline: The Hän are pushed out of their fish camp
entries.digest: The Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in's own heritage account says that within a month of the discovery the Hän were forced out of Tr'ochëk, the salmon camp they had used for centuries, and that mining destroyed the fish traps. The point of land became Lousetown, later Klondike City, with a sawmill, brewery, saloons and a red-light district. No surviving firsthand account by Chief Isaac from these weeks was found.
entries.source_note: Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in, Tr'ochëk heritage page; date range only.

entries.headline: The Discovery claim goes on the register
entries.digest: Carmack recorded the Discovery claim before Inspector Constantine, acting as gold commissioner, and Keish and Káa Goox's claims on either side were entered too. The registration made the claim legally his, whatever was said about who found the gold. Robert Henderson later fought the same office over his own claims.
entries.source_note: DCB, Keish; Robert Henderson's Search for Recognition (canadianmysteries.ca) gives 24 September 1896.

entries.headline: The police inspector enters Carmack's claim
entries.digest: As the only Canadian official in reach, Constantine was recording claims as fast as men came in from the new creek. The registration of Carmack's double Discovery claim passed across his table among dozens of others. His request for a proper gold commissioner went south with his report.
entries.source_note: DCB, Keish (Carmack recorded before Constantine, 24 Sept. 1896).

entries.headline: Henderson learns too late and loses his discovery claim
entries.digest: By the time Henderson heard of Bonanza the rich ground was gone. The recorder ruled that Gold Bottom and Hunker were one creek, so only Andrew Hunker's discovery claim could stand, and Henderson was left with an ordinary claim. He later sold it for 3,000 dollars to meet medical costs.
entries.source_note: Robert Henderson's Search for Recognition (after Whyte, 1998), canadianmysteries.ca.

entries.headline: First official word: a stampede and 338 claims
entries.digest: Constantine reported that Carmack had found coarse gold on Bonanza, a tributary of the 'Trondec', showing about three dollars to the pan, and that men had left their old claims in a stampede. 338 claims had been recorded and about 150 more waited to be entered. He passed on the old-timers' view that it was as rich as early California and asked urgently for a gold commissioner, courts and more men; his post was short of firewood and its earth roofs leaked.
entries.quote: a stampede for the new diggings
entries.source_note: NWMP Report 1896, Appendix DD, dated Fort Constantine 20 Nov. 1896 (ExploreNorth transcription).

entries.headline: Mittens, moccasins and bread for the miners
entries.digest: Through the first winter on the claims Shaaw Tláa sewed mittens and moccasins and baked bread to sell to miners. Over the next four years the family's claims produced close to a million dollars in gold. None of it would remain hers.
entries.source_note: DCB, Shaaw Tláa.

entries.place: Bonanza Creek and the Dawson flat
entries.headline: The surveyor re-chains an overstaked creek
entries.digest: Ogilvie spent the winter surveying the Bonanza claims, where hasty staking had produced overlaps and gaps, and laying out the Dawson townsite for Ladue. The fractions he found between claims became small fortunes for whoever staked them. He came to know every party to the discovery dispute in these months.
entries.source_note: Ogilvie's survey role is standard; months approximate. Early Days on the Yukon (1913).

entries.place: Puget Sound and Schwabacher Wharf, Seattle
entries.headline: Sixty-eight miners and more than a ton of gold
entries.digest: Three days after the Excelsior reached San Francisco with Klondike gold, the Portland passed up the Sound about 3 a.m.; the P-I had met her at sea by tug. By 6 a.m. more than 5,000 people crowded the wharf. The paper's extra cried gold four times, counted sixty-eight rich men and put the cargo at 700,000 dollars; about two tons were actually unloaded. Seattle's mayor, at a convention in San Francisco, wired his resignation and left for the North.
entries.quote: more than a ton of solid gold on board
entries.source_note: HistoryLink 687; Daily Colonist 18 July 1897 reprint of the P-I (ExploreNorth); Excelsior 14 July per ExploreNorth treasure-ships page.

entries.headline: The story crosses the border: 'El Dorado at last'
entries.digest: The Daily Colonist of Victoria reprinted the Post-Intelligencer's report under a stack of headlines: the strike was on the Klondike in Canadian territory, Seattle was wild, Tacoma had the fever. The news, telegraphed east, met a country in depression, and outfitting stores on the coast began to sell out within days.
entries.source_note: Daily Colonist, 18 July 1897, transcribed by ExploreNorth.

entries.headline: Sailing north with Jack London
entries.digest: Thompson's diary opens as the party sailed from San Francisco on the Umatilla. With him were Jack London, 21 and unknown, London's elderly brother-in-law James Shepard, and the partners they gathered on board. They were among the first thousands to leave after the treasure ships came in.
entries.source_note: Huntington JL 1692 (diary, July–Oct 1897); date per National Park Service, Gold Rush Writers.

entries.headline: A Harper's man buys his outfit
entries.digest: About a month after the first gold reached the coast, Harper's Weekly sent Adney north. He bought supplies in Victoria and took ship for Skagway with a 5x7 camera, a pocket Kodak and a developing outfit, leaving glass plates behind as too heavy and fragile.
entries.source_note: Anchorage Daily News (2018) review; NPS, Gold Rush Writers (camera list).

entries.headline: Landed at Dyea, freighting up the Taiya
entries.digest: The party landed on the tide flats at Dyea and began hauling their outfits six miles up the Taiya River by boat. Each man had to move his supplies in relays toward the Chilkoot. Shepard soon gave up and turned home.
entries.source_note: NPS, Gold Rush Writers, following the Thompson diary.

entries.headline: Over the summit after three weeks of packing
entries.digest: By the end of August the party had relayed its tons of goods over the Chilkoot, London carrying heavy loads alongside paid packers. The pass, a staircase of rock and later of cut snow, was the route the Tagish and Tlingit had controlled and packed for a living. On the far side they hauled down to Lake Lindeman.
entries.source_note: NPS, Gold Rush Writers (over the pass by 31 August).

entries.headline: Two boats built, the party sails
entries.digest: Having whipsawed lumber and built two boats, the party sailed from Lindeman. Ahead lay the lakes, Miles Canyon and the White Horse Rapids, which London ran for other stampeders for pay. Winter was weeks away.
entries.source_note: NPS, Gold Rush Writers.

entries.headline: A guide promises the frozen country will repay
entries.digest: Klondyke Nuggets went on sale as the rush gathered, with routes, distances, prices and descriptions of the Yukon seasons. It promised that the summer valley could be a bed of roses and warned of the winter. It said nothing about the people already living at the Klondike mouth.
entries.source_note: Klondyke Nuggets (1897), Project Gutenberg 10043; preface dated September 1897.

entries.headline: Launching a home-made boat in the cold rain
entries.digest: Adney had carried lumber over the pass in near-constant rain, in crowds hauling their goods, and built his own boat at Lindeman. He launched on 5 October, late in a season when ice was already forming on the lakes.
entries.source_note: Anchorage Daily News (2018).

entries.place: Mouth of the Stewart River, 80 miles above Dawson
entries.headline: Stopping short of Dawson for the winter
entries.digest: With the river freezing, the party took over cabins near the mouth of the Stewart, eighty miles upstream from Dawson. London staked a claim nearby that came to nothing. The diary ends that autumn; the winter that followed brought London scurvy and sent him home in 1898 with no gold and the material for his stories.
entries.source_note: NPS, Gold Rush Writers; Huntington JL 1692 (date range July–Oct 1897).

entries.headline: Halloween arrival in a town short of food
entries.digest: Adney reached Dawson on the last day of October, as the river closed. The town that had not existed fifteen months earlier was crowded with men waiting out the winter on uncertain supplies. He spent the winter in cabins in the woods nearby, recording claim staking and winter mining.
entries.source_note: Anchorage Daily News (2018).

entries.headline: A move downriver, agreed with church and government
entries.digest: Over the winter Chief Isaac, church officials and government officials agreed that the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in would move about three miles downriver, and by spring families were building cabins at Moosehide, another traditional camp. The First Nation's account says the move had his consent and cooperation; his daughter later said he feared the gold rush would lead his people into bad habits. No surviving firsthand account by Isaac from that winter was found.
entries.source_note: Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in, Tr'ochëk page; Chief Isaac booklet (Patricia Lindgren interview 1974–75, published 1977).

entries.headline: Superintendent Steele sails north
entries.digest: Steele's diary records arranging freight, boarding the Thistle and sailing at five in heavy seas. Over the next week he passed Seymour Narrows and Queen Charlotte Sound, noted a wreck at Mary Island, and called at Wrangell. He was going north to take charge of the border posts.
entries.source_note: Steele diary 1898 (University of Alberta), entries 1–14 February.

entries.headline: The flag on the Chilkoot, and a ton of goods at the line
entries.digest: Inspector Belcher hoisted the flag at the Chilkoot summit and began collecting customs; Inspector Strickland did the same at the White Pass two days later. Each newcomer had to bring at least 1,150 pounds of food plus tents, utensils and tools, or be turned back. With the rest of the outfit this was roughly a ton, which became the shorthand for the rule.
entries.quote: at least 1,150 pounds of solid food
entries.source_note: Forty Years in Canada (1915), ch. XV. Steele's diary is blank 20 Feb–12 Apr 1898.

entries.place: The Scales, below the Chilkoot summit
entries.headline: Avalanches bury the Chilkoot trail
entries.digest: After days of heavy snow, a series of slides between Sheep Camp and the Scales buried people on the trail, the largest striking a line of packers just before noon. Hundreds dug from Sheep Camp for four days; some were brought out alive. The Dyea paper counted forty-nine dead by 10 April and a citizens' committee recorded each body's effects; later counts run to sixty-five or more. Steele's memoir has a section on the fatal avalanches; his diary is silent for these weeks.
entries.source_note: The Trail (Dyea), 9 April 1898 (Yukon Archives PDF); NPS, Palm Sunday Avalanche; Forty Years in Canada ch. XV contents. Steele was not at the slide.

entries.headline: 1,420 boats waiting for the ice
entries.digest: With about 960 tents at Bennett and boats being built everywhere, Steele counted 1,420 boats between Bennett and Lindeman. The police had begun registering each boat and its crew so that the drowned could be identified and the missing traced.
entries.source_note: Steele diary 1898, 15–21 May.

entries.headline: The ice goes out and the fleet sails
entries.digest: Steele noted that the ice was nearly all out of Lindeman, and the next day many boats sailed down the lakes, too early in his view. From the hill behind his office, his memoir says, he saw over 800 boats under sail on Bennett at once.
entries.source_note: Steele diary 1898, 29–30 May; Forty Years in Canada ch. XV (800 boats).

entries.headline: Rules for the rapids after scores of wrecks
entries.digest: At Miles Canyon Steele found that about 52 boats had been lost in the rapids. He ordered that only competent pilots take boats through and that they report to the police corporal in charge; his memoir adds that women and children were to walk around. The order made the police the masters of the river route.
entries.source_note: Steele diary 1898, 1–10 June; Forty Years in Canada ch. XV (order details).

entries.headline: The Yukon becomes a territory
entries.digest: Parliament's Yukon Territory Act took the Yukon out of the North-West Territories and gave it a Commissioner and an appointed council of up to six. Ottawa had decided that a gold country of tens of thousands could not be run from Regina. Ogilvie, who had surveyed the claims, was named Commissioner that summer.
entries.source_note: Yukon Territory Act, 61 Vict. c. 6, assented 13 June 1898 (ExploreNorth transcription). Ogilvie's appointment month approx.

entries.place: The Chilkoot Trail to Lake Lindeman
entries.headline: The last miles into Lindeman, carried by her brother
entries.digest: Pregnant and in long skirts, Martha Purdy crossed the Chilkoot with her brother. In her memoir the descent to Lindeman was the worst of it: roots and rocks tore her boots and hands, and her brother carried her for much of the final mile. She wrote later that she would never do it again.
entries.source_note: My Seventy Years (1938), excerpt in Mayer, Klondike Women (1989), pp. 102–103, via University of Washington CSPN; month per Canadian Encyclopedia (1898). Digest only.

entries.headline: The summer boom of 1898
entries.digest: Adney watched Dawson fill as the spring fleets arrived: tents on every flat, prices high, gold dust as currency and most newcomers too late for good ground. The town was at its peak; estimates of its population that summer range from under 20,000 to 30,000 or more. He left in the autumn and turned his notes into The Klondike Stampede.
entries.source_note: Anchorage Daily News (2018); population range from canadianmysteries.ca (After the Gold Rush) and Yukon News. Precise peak not verified.

entries.headline: Arrival in Dawson
entries.digest: Martha Purdy reached Dawson after the river journey from the lakes. She stayed on through the winter, with her child due, in a town where women were a small minority.
entries.source_note: Canadian Encyclopedia, Martha Black (arrival 5 August 1898).

entries.headline: Steele takes charge in Dawson
entries.digest: Steele left Bennett by steamer and reached Dawson on 6 September. His September entries are about organising the barracks, hearing cases and constables falling ill. The Yukon command, and the policing of a crowded gold town, were now his.
entries.source_note: Steele diary 1898, 2–30 September.

entries.headline: A son born in a Dawson cabin
entries.digest: In January 1899 Martha Purdy gave birth to her son Lyman in Dawson. In the course of that year, as news of beach gold at Nome spread, many Dawson residents left down the river; she stayed.
entries.source_note: Canadian Encyclopedia (birth January 1899); Nome exodus per canadianmysteries.ca (After the Gold Rush).

entries.headline: A reserve at Moosehide
entries.digest: The Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in heritage account records that a reserve was created at Moosehide for the people's use in 1900. It was a small fraction of the territory the Hän had used, set aside downstream of a town that now stood on their fish camp.
entries.source_note: Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in, Our Heritage page (reserve 1900).

entries.headline: Carmack leaves Shaaw Tláa
entries.digest: In 1900 Carmack married a Dawson woman and left Kate almost penniless in California. She tried several times to go to law against him and gave up.
entries.source_note: DCB, Shaaw Tláa.

entries.headline: Home to Carcross, with nothing from the fortune
entries.digest: Shaaw Tláa returned to Carcross to live with the Tagish people. Her brother built her a cabin near his house; she sewed for tourists and later nursed him through his last illness. No record of any settlement from Carmack has been found.
entries.source_note: DCB, Shaaw Tláa.

entries.headline: Ottawa first refuses Henderson's claim
entries.digest: Through his agent H. J. Woodside, Henderson asked to be compensated as the discoverer of the Klondike. In July 1901 Deputy Minister P. G. Keyes refused. Within about a year the department reversed itself and gave him 2,000 feet of placer ground, which proved largely worthless, and later a salaried post in Dawson.
entries.source_note: Robert Henderson's Search for Recognition (after Whyte, 1998), canadianmysteries.ca.

entries.headline: Visiting the cities the gold built
entries.digest: Sponsored by three Dawson trading companies, Chief Isaac travelled south with his brother Walter Benjamin to San Francisco, Seattle and other coastal cities. He gave interviews warning that the newcomers' changes would upset a balance his ancestors had kept; a Seattle reporter recorded that he was tired of strange sights and wanted to go home to his people.
entries.source_note: Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in Chief Isaac booklet; Yukon News, Chief Isaac and the mass media. Reporters' wording, not his own.

entries.headline: 'All Yukon belong to my papas'
entries.digest: The Dawson Daily News printed Chief Isaac's statement, in reporters' dialect, that the game was gone because white men killed the moose and caribou near Dawson, that the newcomers had taken his people's gold, and that the whole Yukon had belonged to his forefathers. It is the plainest surviving statement of the Hän claim to the land the rush was fought over.
entries.quote: All Yukon belong to my papas.
entries.source_note: Dawson Daily News, 15 Dec. 1911, as quoted by Yukon News and the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in Tr'ochëk page.

entries.headline: The surveyor's verdict on who found the Klondike
entries.digest: In Early Days on the Yukon Ogilvie concluded that Carmack could hardly be credited with the discovery, called Keish reliable, truthful and competent, and gave Henderson the title of discoverer of the Klondike for the work that led to the find. He was candid that miners' prejudice against Carmack's Indigenous partners had shaped how the story was told.
entries.source_note: Ogilvie (1913), excerpt at canadianmysteries.ca; Whyte (1998) via Henderson page.

entries.headline: Keish dies; his fortune held in trust
entries.digest: Keish died at home in Carcross after a long illness. In 1905 he had placed the rest of his fortune in trust; after his death it gave yearly support to Shaaw Tláa, his daughter Daisy and Koołseen, and a substantial sum went into trust for Yukon Indigenous people.
entries.source_note: DCB, Keish.

entries.headline: Shaaw Tláa dies in the influenza epidemic
entries.digest: Shaaw Tláa died at Carcross during an influenza epidemic, the disease that had killed her first husband and daughter. In 2019 the Canadian Mining Hall of Fame inducted her, twenty years after the male discoverers.
entries.source_note: DCB, Shaaw Tláa; Canadian Mining Hall of Fame.

convergences.label: The find on Rabbit Creek: four versions of one afternoon
convergences.note: Keish's account (through Ogilvie) and his nephew's give the find to Keish. Oral tradition gives Shaaw Tláa the first nugget, Carmack's memoir gives it to Carmack, and Ladue's guidebook gives the first gold to Henderson a week later. Henderson, over the hill, was not told at all.

convergences.label: Staking day
convergences.note: Carmack takes the double Discovery claim in his own name while Keish guards the stakes. Ogilvie's notes then record the creek filling up within five days.

convergences.label: The claim goes on the register at Forty Mile
convergences.note: The same office that recorded Carmack's Discovery claim would rule against Henderson's discovery claim on Gold Bottom. Paper and the recorder, not the creek, settled who owned what.

convergences.label: Autumn 1896: a town staked over a fishery
convergences.note: Ladue stakes and names Dawson on the flat by Tr'ochëk; the Hän are forced from their salmon camp. Constantine's report counts claims and asks for courts, and does not mention them.

convergences.label: The treasure ships and the first wave
convergences.note: Within a fortnight of the Portland's arrival Jack London's party and the Harper's correspondent were at sea, and Ladue's guidebook was in press. The newspaper story made the stampede.

convergences.label: Autumn 1897: racing the freeze
convergences.note: Thompson's party stops at the Stewart on 9 October; Adney, launching at Lindeman on 5 October, gets through to Dawson on 31 October as the river closes.

convergences.label: Winter 1897–98: the move to Moosehide
convergences.note: While Adney winters in the woods near Dawson recording mining, the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in agree to move downstream. Only one of these winters is told in its participant's own words.

convergences.label: Summer 1898: the territory, the fleet and the peak
convergences.note: Steele's boats come down from Bennett and Ottawa creates the Yukon Territory with Ogilvie as Commissioner. Martha Purdy crosses the pass, and Adney watches Dawson reach its height.

convergences.label: September 1898: the police and the commissioner in Dawson
convergences.note: Steele arrives to take charge of the Dawson barracks a month after Purdy reached the town; Ogilvie arrives as its first Commissioner the same season.

ties.note: Brother and sister; his search for her in 1896 brought the party to the Klondike mouth, and he built her a cabin at Carcross after Carmack left her.
Uncle and nephew; Koołseen travelled with him in 1896 and was supported by his estate after 1916.
Married from the late 1880s; he left her in California in 1900 and she received nothing from the claims.
Partners in the strike; Carmack staked Discovery in his own name and assigned Keish a half-interest, by Ogilvie's account.
Met at the Klondike mouth in August 1896; Henderson's tip and his refusal to share with Carmack's Tagish partners shaped the dispute that followed.
Ogilvie interviewed Keish and Káa Goox separately and together and judged Keish truthful.
Ogilvie knew Henderson personally and backed his claim to be the discoverer of the Klondike, which helped him win a government post.
Ladue's Ogilvie post grubstaked Henderson; Ladue's 1897 book credits Henderson with the first gold.
Ogilvie laid out the Dawson townsite that Ladue had staked.
Carmack recorded the Discovery claim before Constantine on 24 September 1896.
Officers of the same force; Constantine's small detachment of 1895 became the much larger Yukon command Steele led from 1898.
Ladue's townsite of Dawson was laid out beside and over the Hän fish camp at Tr'ochëk.
Both crossed the Chilkoot and built boats at Lake Lindeman in autumn 1897, weeks apart.
Thompson and London sailed eight days after the Portland's arrival made headlines along the coast.

Carmack's Discovery claim recorded at Forty Mile before Constantine as acting gold commissioner.
Recorder rules Gold Bottom and Hunker one creek; Henderson denied a discovery claim; his Hunker claim later sold for $3,000.
338 claims registered, about 150 more to enter; Bonanza prospects $3 to the pan; 1896 output from older creeks about $300,000 (17,647 oz).

threads_out.note: Constantine's first report passed on the old-timers' judgment that Bonanza was as rich as California in the early days, and many Yukon miners, Carmack among them, came from California. San Francisco, where the Excelsior docked, was the city the 1848 rush had built.

Klondike gold reached the markets in 1897–1900 alongside the Rand's deep-level output. Together the two fields ended the gold shortage of the early 1890s and took some of the force out of the free-silver campaign in the United States.

The new gold of the Klondike and the Rand helped the United States formally adopt the gold standard in the Gold Standard Act of 1900. That standard was finally abandoned when the dollar's convertibility into gold ended in 1971.

Shaaw Tláa died at Carcross in March 1920 during an influenza epidemic in the years of the great pandemic. Influenza had earlier killed her first husband and child, and it later killed Chief Isaac in 1932.
